claims.text: The initially solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are single-phase.
Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu are initially homogeneously distributed in the nanoparticles.
Surface segregation of Cu governs the early onset and progression of premelting and melting.
Cu has a lower melting point than Fe, Ni, Cr, and Co.
Cu has lower cohesive energy or weaker bonding than Fe, Ni, Cr, and Co.
Heating causes Cu to preferentially diffuse to the nanoparticle surface.
Cu segregation produces a Cu-enriched, liquid-like interfacial layer.
The Cu-rich interfacial layer melts locally at a temperature below the bulk melting temperature.
The locally molten Cu-rich layer nucleates melting of the nanoparticle.
Melting initiated at the Cu-rich surface propagates inward and accelerates the overall transformation.
Equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles will begin surface melting at a lower temperature than Cu-reduced nanoparticles.
Reducing the Cu fraction will delay surface-melting onset and raise the apparent melting point.
Replacing Cu with a higher-melting-point element such as Pd will delay surface-melting onset and raise the apparent melting point.
The equiatomic nanoparticles will exhibit an inward-moving melting front originating at a Cu-enriched boundary.
A system without significant surface segregation or with less Cu will have a higher premelting-onset temperature and more uniform melting behavior.
Oxidation and uncontrolled kinetic or particle-size effects could obscure the proposed segregation-controlled response.
